Crystal impurities, such as atomic vacancies, are known to modulate the charge transport characteristics of two-dimensional (2D) materials. Here, we apply a first-principles-enriched tight-binding modelling approach to assess the influence of sulfur vacancies on the electronic structure and quantum transport characteristics of MoS2 monolayers. To this end, an sp3d5 orthogonal tight-binding (oTB) model of the pristine and defective MoS2 monolayer is mapped with electronic structure calculations performed at the density functional theory level and subsequently used in the real-space Kubo–Greenwood (KG) scheme for charge transport simulations. Our oTB/KG simulations predict a drop of mobility by two orders of magnitude when the vacancy concentration is increased from 0.1 to 3%, in excellent agreement with experimental results. The simulation of realistic samples (including specific types of defects) pave a new route toward the accurate understanding and the possible prediction of 2D materials for nanoelectronic devices. fetched_contents.text: Recent Progress in the Synthesis of MoS2 Thin Films for Sensing, Photovoltaic and Plasmonic Applications: A Review Abstract In the surge of recent successes of 2D materials following the rise of graphene, molybdenum disulfide (2D-MoS2) has been attracting growing attention from both fundamental and applications viewpoints, owing to the combination of its unique nanoscale properties. For instance, the bandgap of 2D-MoS2, which changes from direct (in the bulk form) to indirect for ultrathin films (few layers), offers new prospects for various applications in optoelectronics. In this review, we present the latest scientific advances in the field of synthesis and characterization of 2D-MoS2 films while highlighting some of their applications in energy harvesting, gas sensing, and plasmonic devices. A survey of the physical and chemical processing routes of 2D-MoS2 is presented first, followed by a detailed description and listing of the most relevant characterization techniques used to study the MoS2 nanomaterial as well as theoretical simulations of its interesting optical properties. Finally, the challenges related to the synthesis of high quality and fairly controllable MoS2 thin films are discussed along with their integration into novel functional devices. Keywords: layered materials, 2D-MoS2, pulsed laser deposition, chemical vapor deposition, photovoltaic, gas sensors, plasmonics 1. Introduction Two-dimensional (2D) materials are generally defined as crystalline substances with a few atoms thickness [1]. Graphene was the first 2D crystal to be ever isolated in 2004 and has since been extensively investigated by many groups around the world [2,3,4,5,6]. In fact, graphene became known as the material of superlatives showing a mechanical strength hundreds of times larger than steel [7] while maintaining a high mechanical flexibility [8] and superior electrical and thermal conductivities [9]. Following the discovery of grapheme [10], a very large spectrum of 2D materials possessing a wide range of highly attractive properties have emerged [8,10]. For instance, two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenide (2D-TMDs) semiconducting (SC) materials have exhibited unique optical and electrical properties [11,12], resulting from the quantum confinement effect attributed to their shapes and sizes with respect to the Bohr radius [13,14,15,16,17], in addition to their surface effects, which is due to the transition from an indirect bandgap in the “bulk form” to a direct bandgap for the “mono- to few-layer” ultrathin film form [18]. The layered configuration of the 2D-TMDs materials is at the origin of their strong interaction with light [19] and the relatively high mobility of their charge carriers [20], which in turn prompted their use in many optoelectronic applications, such as ultra-thin field-effect transistors [21], photo-detectors [22], light emitting diode [23], and solar-cells [24]. Generally, 2D-TMDs form a family of graphite-like layered thin semiconducting structures with the chemical formula of MX2, where M refers to a transition metal atom (Mo, W, etc.) and X is a chalcogen atom (Se, S, etc.). The layered nature of this class of 2D materials induces a strong anisotropy in their electrical, chemical, mechanical, and thermal properties. In particular, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) is the most studied layered 2D-TMD [25,26,27,28,29,30]. From a crystalline point of view, layered MoS2 exists in three polymorphic crystalline structures: 1T (tetragonal) [31], 2H (hexagonal) [32], and 3R (rhombohedral) [33] (Figure 1). The crystallographic parameters associated to these crystalline forms are summarized in Table 1. In the case of mono- to few-layer structures, 2H-MoS2 is the most thermodynamically stable phase and thus the most commonly encountered. When the MoS2 is in the monolayer form, it takes an octahedral or a trigonal prismatic coordination phase. Table 1. Crystal parameters and the nature of polymorphic structures of 2D-MoS2. C3v Semiconductor [33] Furthermore, MoS2 layered materials were observed to exhibit various shapes and morphologies, such as planar [34,35,36] and vertically aligned nanosheets (NSs) [37], nanoflowers [38], nanotubes [39], nanowires [40], and nanoplatelets [41,42]. This variety of forms could be controlled by choosing suitable synthesis routes with optimized operating parameters [38,39,40,41,43,44,45,46,47]. Main defect classes in MoS₂ and their negative effects on device performance

The evidence points to three primary defect classes in MoS₂ that degrade performance: sulfur vacancies, metal vacancies, and impurities. Sulfur vacancies are the most prevalent defects in MoS₂, described as instances of missing single sulfur atoms [N4-R5]. The same evidence also states that sulfur vacancies can appear as isolated defects or as clusters on one or both sides, and that sulfur vacancy concentration affects defect-state broadening through interacting sulfur vacancies [N1-R3]. This means sulfur vacancies are not only abundant but also can cluster and interact, amplifying their impact.

Metal vacancies, while less explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, are still relevant as a defect class because the evidence explicitly mentions crystal impurities such as atomic vacancies [N1-F1]. The broader defect family includes interstitials and substitutional defects, even though the provided excerpts do not exhaustively enumerate them all. The evidence on MoS₂ synthesis methods also highlights point defects in general, including Mo and S vacancies and charged versions of these defects [N5-F3], suggesting a broader defect landscape than just sulfur vacancies.

Each defect class modifies the electronic band structure and carrier behavior in distinct ways. Sulfur vacancies are especially important because they shift the electronic structure and affect charge transport. The evidence on defective MoS₂ shows that sulfur vacancies modulate charge transport characteristics and that carrier mobility is sensitive to both vacancy density and spatial arrangement [N1-F1]. A first-principles study further reports that mobility drops by two orders of magnitude when vacancy concentration increases from 0.1 to 3%, consistent with experimental results [N1-F1]. This directly ties sulfur vacancies to reduced mobility. The same evidence also states that vacancy concentration changes the broadening of defect states [N1-R3], indicating a distortion of the band structure near defect sites.

Structural defects more generally act as charge traps, scattering centers, and transport barriers, reducing carrier mobility, causing localized charge accumulation, and creating spatially inhomogeneous charge distribution [N3-F4]. In hopping conduction, charge carriers move through localized defect/trap states via nearest neighbor hopping and variable-range hopping [N3-R3]. This mechanism shows how defects do not merely scatter carriers but also alter transport pathways and trapping behavior. The evidence also notes that defects can remove barriers imposed by trapped states at higher temperature, allowing charge carriers to move freely between defect states [N3-R1], which implies that defects can both restrict and, under certain conditions, temporarily release mobility, depending on thermal energy and defect distribution.

The performance consequences are specific and severe. Reduced mobility is the most directly stated consequence [N1-F1][N3-F4]. Defects also increase leakage by acting as charge traps and scattering centers [N3-F4]. The evidence further links defects to instability and degradation: defects can weaken in-plane vibrations and restoring forces in MoS₂, weakening the Mo–S bonds and introducing structural fragility [N6-R2]. In addition, sulfur vacancies can weaken the in-plane vibration in the Mo–S bonds, leading to a weaker restoring force and likely to reduced mechanical stability and structural integrity [N6-R2]. The evidence also reports that sulfur vacancies can lead to low photoluminescence emission [N6-R4], indicating optoelectronic loss.

In summary, the main defect classes are sulfur vacancies, metal vacancies, and other point defects, with sulfur vacancies being the most prevalent and most damaging. Sulfur vacancies modify the band structure and defect-state distribution, reduce mobility, and increase trapping and scattering; structural defects in general reduce mobility, create charge traps, and cause instability and degradation. The evidence supports a strong causal chain from defects to reduced carrier transport, to optoelectronic loss, and to device instability [N1-F1][N3-F4][N4-R5][N6-R2].

Relationship between defects and device-level performance in MoS₂-based systems

Defects in MoS₂ strongly limit carrier transport by acting as scattering centers and traps. Structural defects are described as charge traps, scattering centers, and transport barriers, giving rise to reduced carrier mobility, localized charge accumulation, and spatially inhomogeneous charge distribution [N3-F4]. This means that defects do not merely reduce conductivity in a simple linear fashion; instead, they fragment the transport path, localize charge, and create non-uniform current flow. The evidence also notes that defects can remove barriers imposed by trapped states at higher temperature, allowing charge carriers to move freely between defect states [N3-R1]. This suggests that defect-induced transport limitations are not always static but can be temperature-dependent, with higher temperatures temporarily reducing the effective trapping barrier.

The transport consequences are clear: reduced mobility is a central performance loss, with the evidence showing mobility dropping by two orders of magnitude when vacancy concentration increases from 0.1 to 3% [N1-F1]. Structural defects also reduce carrier mobility directly [N3-F4]. The evidence further indicates that defects can increase leakage by acting as charge traps and scattering centers [N3-F4]. This matters because leakage degrades device performance by reducing the on/off ratio and increasing power dissipation. The same evidence also connects defects to hysteresis and degraded switching behavior, emphasizing that defect-induced charge trapping can make device operation non-repeatable and less reliable [N3-F4].

Optoelectronic effects are equally important. The evidence states that sulfur vacancies can lead to low photoluminescence emission [N6-R4], which directly links defects to optoelectronic loss. It also notes that defect-state broadening occurs with interacting sulfur vacancies [N1-R3], which would broaden the optical response and reduce photoluminescence efficiency by scattering photons and altering the density of states near the bandgap. The evidence on MoS₂ synthesis methods further highlights that sulfur vacancies and charged vacancies are intrinsic point defects that strongly affect charge transport and film quality [N5-F3]. This implies that defect density controls not only electrical but also optical performance.

Device stability and reliability issues are tied to defect-induced degradation. The evidence reports that sulfur vacancies weaken in-plane vibrations and restoring forces in MoS₂, weakening the Mo–S bonds and introducing structural fragility [N6-R2]. This fragility can cause mechanical instability and possibly accelerate degradation under operation. The same evidence also notes that sulfur vacancies can lead to high n-type doping behavior, implying that defects can alter the surface and bulk electronic environment in ways that degrade device behavior [N6-R4]. The evidence on collapsed MoS₂ nanotubes emphasizes that defects and surface damage can arise during device fabrication or operation, leading to significant degradation in performance, stability, and operational lifetime [N3-F4]. It also highlights hysteresis as a degradation effect, which is a reliability issue because it affects switching behavior and makes devices less predictable [N3-F4].

Taken together, defects in MoS₂-based systems limit carrier transport by scattering and trapping, reduce mobility, increase leakage, and cause instability and hysteresis. They also degrade optoelectronic performance by lowering photoluminescence and broadening defect states, while defect-induced mechanical fragility and surface doping changes can reduce device reliability and lifetime [N1-F1][N3-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4].

How synthesis methods create or suppress defects in MoS₂

The evidence identifies several synthesis methods and explains how each creates or suppresses defects. Micromechanical exfoliation is described as offering the highest material quality but being limited by yield, so it is mainly used for basic research [N2-R3]. This suggests that exfoliation can produce high-quality MoS₂, but the method is not scalable for defect-suppressed bulk production. Liquid-phase exfoliation is also mentioned, but the evidence does not provide details on its defect behavior, so it should be treated as a general synthesis route rather than a defect-specific one [N2-R3].

Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) is highlighted as one of the most popular routes for large-scale, high-quality, and low-cost 2D-MoS₂ production [N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that CVD has proven particularly challenging because of non-uniform precursor vapor pressure, which leads to the formation of various defects, including point defects in the film [N5-F3]. This is a direct defect-formation mechanism for CVD: non-uniform precursor vapor distribution creates conditions where defects nucleate and grow. The same evidence states that the major difference in field-effect transistor performance under optimal and sulfur-rich conditions is degradation of field-effect mobility and current switching ratio, attributed to increased carrier scattering at charged vacancy defect sites [N5-F3]. This shows that CVD conditions can either suppress defects under optimal precursor pressure or create defects when precursor pressure is unbalanced.

Sputter-CVD is presented as a viable method to synthesize large-area, high-quality, and layer-controlled MoS₂ that can be adapted for applications [N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that pulsed DC magnetron sputtering has been used to deposit bulk, monolayer, and few-layers of MoS₂ films [N2-R5]. These sputter-based methods can produce high-quality films, but the evidence does not explicitly state whether they suppress defects better than CVD. It does emphasize that sputter-CVD can be adapted for layer control, which is important because defect control often depends on thickness and layer quality [N2-R4]. The evidence on CVD-grown MoS₂ also notes that films grown under optimum and sulfur-rich conditions have lower carrier concentration and different FET performance, suggesting that sputter-CVD may be better at controlling precursor chemistry than conventional CVD [N5-F3].

The evidence also indicates that synthesis-method residues or byproducts can contribute to defects. The CVD evidence explicitly states that defects under study are Mo and S vacancies and charged versions of these defects, and that CVD growth typically happens in conditions where there is either an excess or a deficit of S atoms [N5-F3]. This implies that precursor chemistry and byproduct chemistry are defect sources. The evidence on MoS₂ synthesis methods further notes that sulfur vacancies are the most prevalent defects, and that sulfur vacancy concentration changes defect-state broadening through interacting sulfur vacancies [N1-R3]. This supports the idea that byproduct chemistry and precursor balance are not just secondary effects but intrinsic defect sources.

Conditions that favor high-quality versus defect-rich MoS₂ are clear. Micromechanical exfoliation favors high material quality but is limited in scalability [N2-R3]. CVD can produce large-area, high-quality films, but defects are favored when precursor vapor pressure is non-uniform [N5-F3]. Optimum precursor pressure conditions suppress defect-related mobility degradation, while sulfur-rich conditions still produce defects, albeit with different carrier behavior [N5-F3]. The evidence also states that the MoS₂ films grown by CVD mostly exist in the 2H phase, which is believed to be the most thermodynamically stable phase [N5-F3]. This suggests that thermodynamic stability is a quality factor, but even stable growth conditions can produce defects if precursor chemistry is not controlled.

Pressure is also significant. The evidence on pressure and temperature effects on structural stability reports that high-pressure experiments show pressure-induced isostructural hexagonal behavior, while the crystal structure of MoS₂ is stable on increasing temperature [N5-R2]. This suggests that pressure can stabilize different structural states and may indirectly influence defect density by altering the thermodynamic competition between phases. The evidence on low-temperature solid-source synthesis notes that the results provide a path toward high-quality, thermal-budget-compatible 2D semiconductors [N5-R5]. This supports the idea that lower temperatures can suppress defects, but the evidence also implies that thermal budget compatibility requires careful control rather than simply lowering temperature alone.

Ambient atmosphere and precursor chemistry are central to defect control. The evidence on MoS₂ synthesis methods emphasizes that precursor vapor pressure is the dominant factor controlling defect concentrations [N5-F3]. It also states that the major difference in FET performance under optimum and sulfur-rich conditions is degradation of field-effect mobility and current switching ratio, attributed to increased carrier scattering at charged vacancy defect sites [N5-F3]. This means that atmosphere and precursor chemistry are not only thermodynamic inputs but also direct defect sources. The evidence on gaseous precursor-induced vacancy defect control explicitly states that increasing sulfur vapor pressure transformed the film morphology and that non-uniform precursor vapor distribution promoted the formation of intrinsic point defects [N5-F3]. It further reports that optimum and sulfur-rich conditions yielded different carrier concentrations and FET performance, demonstrating that ambient conditions can either suppress or enhance defect-related mobility degradation [N5-F3].

Thermodynamic models link synthesis parameters to defect formation in a concrete way. The evidence explicitly states that a thermodynamic model was developed to link growth parameters to native defect formation, and that the analysis considered Mo and S vacancies in both neutral and charged states with equilibrium concentrations determined from defect formation reactions [N5-R1]. The same evidence also states that the model validated experimental observations, showing that growth parameters are not just empirical factors but can be predicted and controlled using thermodynamics [N5-R1]. This is a strong point: synthesis parameters are not arbitrary; they are thermodynamically linked to defect formation.

### Conditions that minimize or maximize defect density during film growth

The evidence identifies conditions that minimize or maximize defect density. **Optimum precursor pressure conditions** suppress defect-related mobility degradation [N5-F3]. In contrast, **sulfur-rich conditions** still produce defects, albeit with different carrier behavior [N5-F3]. The evidence on MoS₂ synthesis methods also notes that the MoS₂ films grown by CVD mostly exist in the 2H phase, which is believed to be the most thermodynamically stable phase [N5-F3]. This suggests that thermodynamic stability favors a lower-defect phase, but defect formation can still occur if precursor chemistry is imbalanced. The evidence on low-temperature solid-source synthesis supports the idea that controlled thermal budgets can produce high-quality materials, while conventional CVD can produce defect-rich films with lower carrier mobility [N5-F3][N5-R5].

## Integrated conclusion

The main defects in MoS₂ that negatively impact device performance are **sulfur vacancies**, **metal vacancies**, and other point defects, with sulfur vacancies being the most prevalent and most damaging. These defects modify the electronic band structure and carrier behavior by reducing mobility, increasing trapping and scattering, and broadening defect states. The consequences are reduced mobility, increased leakage, instability, degradation, and optoelectronic loss [N1-F1][N3-F4][N4-R5][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Synthesis methods influence defect formation in different ways. **Exfoliation** tends to give high quality but limited yield; **CVD** is scalable but can produce point defects when precursor vapor pressure is uneven; **sputter-CVD** is viable for high-quality, layer-controlled growth; and precursor chemistry, byproduct chemistry, and precursor pressure strongly influence defect formation [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5][N5-F3]. Conditions that favor high-quality MoS₂ include optimum precursor pressure, while sulfur-rich or unbalanced conditions can create defects that degrade FET performance [N5-F3].

Growth conditions and synthesis parameters control defect formation through temperature, pressure, and ambient atmosphere. Thermodynamic models explicitly link these parameters to native defect formation, and the evidence shows that optimum conditions can suppress defect-related mobility degradation, while sulfur-rich or unbalanced conditions can create defects that degrade FET performance [N5-R1][N5-F3][N5-R2][N5-R5]. In short, MoS₂ quality and defect density are not fixed by synthesis method alone; they depend on careful control of precursor chemistry, growth environment, and thermodynamic conditions [N5-F3][N5-R1].
